prompt: Why does `bench.py` hold every model to one processor?
hint: Think about what the clock is meant to compare.

choices.text: Because scikit-learn's models crash with more than one thread
choices.why: They run on four; the program limits them by choice, not to avoid a failure.

choices.text: Because the five folds would otherwise run in parallel and mix their scores
choices.why: The folds run one after another in a plain `for` loop whatever the thread count.

choices.text: Because a network trains faster on one processor than on four
choices.why: Speed was not the reason given; fairness of the comparison was.

choices.text: So the clock measures the work, not the thread handling
choices.why: Right. With four processors each library divides its work its own way, and on a busy machine that division costs more than the work.

prompt: On the breast cancer table the three models scored 0.979, 0.970 and 0.967, with about 114 tumours in each fold. What is the fair reading?
hint: How many tumours is one point?

choices.text: Logistic regression is the better model, by 1.2 points
choices.why: 1.2 points is one or two tumours a fold, too small to call from one run of each (lesson 18).

choices.text: The network lost because 569 rows are too few to train any model
choices.why: All three trained well past the 63% majority class, so the rows were enough.

choices.text: They differ by a tumour or two a fold, and the network bought nothing
choices.why: Right. No model has clearly won on accuracy, and the network was the slowest.

choices.text: Boosting failed, because 0.970 is below what the majority class scores
choices.why: The majority class scores 0.63 here, far below all three.

prompt: A table of 50,000 loan applications has 40 columns chosen by analysts. After a week of tuning, a network scores 0.912; boosting with its defaults scored 0.915 on the same folds. What does this lesson recommend?
hint: Which model is cheaper to train, to rerun and to explain?

choices.text: Keep boosting
choices.why: Right. The network has not beaten the baseline, and it costs more at every step.

choices.text: Keep the network, since it is close and will improve with more tuning
choices.why: More tuning is more weeks, and boosting got its score with none.

choices.text: Average the two models' scores and report 0.9135
choices.why: An average of two scores is not a model anybody can deploy.

choices.text: Switch to logistic regression, since it won on the cancer table
choices.why: Winning on one table says nothing about this one; it would have to be run here.

prompt: In `table.py`, a monthly customer under 24 months of tenure leaves. Why does a tree capture that rule more easily than a network?
hint: Think about the shape of the rule: a step.

choices.text: Trees see more rows of training data than networks do
choices.why: Both saw the same 2,400 rows of each fold.

choices.text: Trees standardise the columns first
choices.why: It is the network that needs standardising; a split on a column does not care about its scale.

choices.text: The network was given no access to the tenure column
choices.why: All ten columns went to all three models.

choices.text: A split lands exactly on 24; a network builds the step out of smooth ReLU pieces
choices.why: Right. Sharp thresholds and their `and` are what trees are made of, and what networks approximate slowly.

prompt: In `bench.py`'s network, each of `table.py`'s five noise columns has a weight into each of the 64 first-layer units. How many weights is that in total?
hint: Columns times units.

prompt: You add 20 more columns of pure noise to `table.py` and rerun the bench. Between boosting and the network, which does this lesson's argument expect to lose more accuracy?
hint: Who has to learn to ignore a column, and with how many numbers?

choices.text: Boosting, because it has more columns to try splits on
choices.why: Trying a split on a useless column costs time, and the split is simply not chosen.

choices.text: The network, which has 1,280 new weights to silence from the same rows
choices.why: Right: 20 columns times 64 units, learnt from 2,400 rows, with room to fit noise.

choices.text: Neither, since noise columns average out to zero
choices.why: Their mean is near zero, but each row's values are not, and a model can fit them.

choices.text: Both equally, since both see exactly the same rows
choices.why: The same rows meet two very different ways of using a column.

prompt: With 2 images of each digit to train on, which model did best on the 360 validation images?
hint: Look at the first row of `small.py`'s output.

choices.text: Lesson 11's CNN
choices.why: It was last, at 0.717.

choices.text: Lesson 9's MLP
choices.why: Close, at 0.761, but still behind.

choices.text: All three tied, at 0.764
choices.why: Only logistic regression reached 0.764; the others were below.

choices.text: Logistic regression
choices.why: Right, at 0.764, with 650 weights against the CNN's 38,282.

prompt: Why does `small.py` give every size of training set the same 1,020 optimiser steps?
hint: What would 30 epochs mean for 20 images?

choices.text: Because 1,020 is close to the number of training images
choices.why: The number comes from 34 batches times 30 epochs, lesson 9's recipe.

choices.text: To make the small sets overfit on purpose
choices.why: Overfitting is a risk of the setup, not its aim.

choices.text: So no network loses for having been stopped early
choices.why: Right. Thirty epochs of 20 images would be 30 steps, and the network would lose for lack of training rather than lack of data.

choices.text: Because SGD at 0.1 needs exactly 1,020 steps to converge
choices.why: No rate converges in a fixed number of steps; 1,020 is borrowed from lesson 9.

prompt: Deep learning's own answer to little data is to start from a ___ model and train a new head on the few examples.
hint: Lessons 13 and 17.

prompt: Put the lesson's recipe for a new table in the order it is run.
hint: From the floor up.
items: A linear model on standardised columns
Gradient boosting with its defaults, on the table as it came
A network, which has to beat boosting by more than the spread

prompt: In `baseline.py`, why did the plain logistic regression pipeline refuse the table while boosting ran?
hint: Read the refusal.

choices.text: `StandardScaler` failed on a column of money
choices.why: The message came from `LogisticRegression`, not from the scaler.

choices.text: A fifth of the charges were `NaN`, which it does not accept
choices.why: Right. Boosting learns which side of each split the blanks go to; logistic regression needs them filled first.

choices.text: Logistic regression handles two classes and this table has three
choices.why: The label is leave or stay, two classes.

choices.text: `cross_val_score` gives a model with no `random_state` a refusal
choices.why: The imputed pipeline had none either and ran, at 0.797.

prompt: A new table has a `country` column with 80 values and blanks in a third of its `income` column. Which first model run follows the lesson's recipe after the majority class and a linear model?
hint: Step 3 says: as it came.

choices.text: Impute, one-hot encode and scale everything, then train an MLP to find the ceiling
choices.why: That is a network before the baseline exists, which is the habit the recipe exists to stop.

choices.text: Drop every row with a blank, so all models see complete data
choices.why: That throws away a third of the rows, and boosting needed none of them dropped.

choices.text: Boosting on the table as it is, told which column is a category
choices.why: Right. It takes the blanks natively, and categories only need naming.

choices.text: XGBoost, because scikit-learn's boosting refuses categories
choices.why: `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accepts categorical columns once told which they are.

prompt: In `moved.py`, which model kept the most accuracy when the validation digits moved one pixel to the right?
hint: Compare the line `moved +1`.

choices.text: Gradient boosting, at 0.425
choices.why: Boosting fell from 0.978 to 0.425.

choices.text: None of them, all three stayed above 0.95
choices.why: All three dropped; only the CNN stayed above 0.7.

choices.text: Logistic regression, at 0.381
choices.why: It was the lowest of the three.

choices.text: The CNN, at 0.706
choices.why: Right. Its filters are the same weights at every place, so a moved stroke is still found.

prompt: Why did boosting fall from 0.978 to 0.425 on digits moved by one pixel?
hint: What did its splits look at?

choices.text: Its splits test fixed pixel positions, so a moved digit is a different table
choices.why: Right. Nothing it learnt about pixel 27 carries over to pixel 28.

choices.text: It overfitted the 1,077 training digits far more than the CNN did on the same images
choices.why: On the digits in place it scored 0.978, equal to the CNN, so it generalised as well there.

choices.text: The blank column moved in confused its handling of missing values
choices.why: Blank is 0 ink, not `NaN`; nothing was missing.

choices.text: Boosting needs at least 1,000 rows per class
choices.why: It trained on the same 1,077 images as the CNN and tied it before the move.

prompt: A network beats boosting by 0.4 points, and five seeds of the same network spread over 1 point. What does the checklist say?
hint: Lesson 18's row.

choices.text: It has not won; keep the cheaper model
choices.why: Right. The difference is smaller than what a change of seed moves.

choices.text: The network has won, by 0.4 points
choices.why: A lead inside the spread is not a lead anyone has measured.

choices.text: Train the network for more epochs until the lead passes 1 point
choices.why: Training until a number looks good is choosing on noise.

choices.text: Report the best seed, since that is what the network can reach
choices.why: The best of five is a lucky draw, not what the next run will give.

prompt: A clinic has 30 labelled X-ray images per class and wants a classifier. Which plan follows the checklist?
hint: Two rows apply: raw input, and little data.

choices.text: Boosting on the raw pixels, because there is little data
choices.why: Pixels are not columns a tree splits well; `moved.py` showed how brittle that is.

choices.text: A CNN trained from scratch for many epochs
choices.why: With 30 per class, `small.py`'s CNN came last; more epochs only memorise.

choices.text: A network pretrained on many images, with a new head trained on the 30
choices.why: Right. The input needs learnt features and the data is too small to learn them, so they come from elsewhere.

choices.text: Logistic regression on the raw pixels, since it won with 20 digits
choices.why: It won against networks trained from nothing; a pretrained one was not in that race.

prompt: `table.py` makes 3,000 rows and `bench.py` uses five folds. How many rows does each model train on in one fold?
hint: Four folds of the five.

prompt: On the digits in place, boosting and the CNN both scored 0.978. What does that tie say?
hint: How many numbers is an 8 by 8 image?

choices.text: Convolution brings nothing to images
choices.why: One pixel of movement showed what it brings: 0.706 against 0.425.

choices.text: At 64 pixels, an image is small enough to be handled as a table
choices.why: Right. The case for a network grows with the input, a photograph being 150,528 numbers.

choices.text: Boosting has learnt to find strokes anywhere in the image
choices.why: Moved by one pixel it fell to 0.425, so it had learnt fixed positions.

choices.text: The validation set is too easy to separate any two models
choices.why: The same set separated logistic regression, at 0.967, from both.

choices.text: Boosting refused the table with missing charges
